metric_rationale: The design contains three families of trials on which a lexicographic one-reason rule and a unit-weight counting rule make opposite (or differently determinate) commitments: (i) pairs 1-4, where the single top cue is pitted against a coalition of 1-4 lower cues; (ii) pairs 9-12, where the first discriminating cue sits lower in the cascade and all remaining cues favour the other option; and (iii) pairs 5-6, where the tally is exactly even so a counting rule must guess at 50/50 whatever its parameters, while the cue cascade is fully decisive. The metric pools exactly these trials (agreement controls 7-8 are excluded, since both rules pick the same option there and they only dilute the contrast) and reports the proportion of choices going to the option favoured by the first discriminating cue. Under Take The Best this is (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2 on every included trial, i.e. high (~0.85 averaged over the parameter ranges) and tight, because each subject contributes 80 trials. Under Tallying it is the complement of the tally-consistent probability on the directional-conflict trials (~0.09) and exactly 0.5 on the two tie pairs, giving ~0.17 overall. Both theories' per-subject spread is driven mainly by the lapse rate, which shifts the two values toward 0.5 by comparable, modest amounts, so the ~0.68 mean gap dwarfs the between-subject variance. Mirror-image pairs are included in equal numbers, so any A/B key bias cancels and cannot inflate or deflate the score for either theory.

Two diagnostic trial families are contrasted within subject, which cancels overall lapse/noise level and sharpens the model split.

(1) Tally-tie trials (pairs 7/8 and 9/10): each option wins exactly the same number of cues, so Tallying is forced to exactly 50/50 for ANY beta and epsilon, while TTB is decisive (cue .93 beats cue .60; cue .87 beats cues .78/.70). I score the proportion of choices for the TTB-designated winner here: 0.5 under Tallying (only binomial jitter over 24 trials), ~0.85 under TTB.

(2) Large-margin disagreement trials (pairs 3/4, 5/6, 11/12): the tally favours the coalition option by 2-4 cues while TTB's top discriminating cue favours the other option. I score the proportion of choices for the tally winner: high (~0.85-0.95) under Tallying because the softmax is driven by beta*margin, near 0.15 under TTB.

The metric is the difference (2) - (1). Tallying predicts a clearly positive value (~+0.35); TTB predicts a strongly negative value (~-0.70), and because under TTB both terms are driven by the same beta and epsilon they move in opposite directions, amplifying rather than blurring the gap. The tie term is parameter-free for Tallying, so my side's variance is dominated by binomial noise alone, keeping the per-subject estimate tight at N=25.

The metric is a parameter-free behavioural index restricted to trials where the two options win on EXACTLY the same number of cues (unit-tally ties) but where the validity-weighted margin is clearly non-zero (|d| >= 0.15 with squared validities; this selects the base pairs {H1,H2} vs {L2,L3}, {H1,L1} vs {M,L3}, {H2,L1} vs {M,L2} and their A/B mirrors, and discards the near-zero-margin pair {H1,L3} vs {H2,L1}). On these trials I score the proportion of choices for the option holding the higher-validity cue set.

Tallying's softmax over equal tallies is EXACTLY uniform for every value of beta and epsilon, so it predicts 0.50 with no parameter-driven between-subject spread at all (only binomial noise over ~36 such trials, var ~0.007). AVAI, in contrast, integrates the continuous weighted difference, so it should land at ~0.89-0.98 across the plausible gamma/beta ranges, again with small between-subject spread. The mean gap is ~0.43 with per-subject SDs under 0.09, giving a decisive Welch test at N=25. It is not trivially true of AVAI: any model that binarises cue-wise winners (Tallying, Equal-Weight on signs, coin-flip-on-ties) must yield 0.5, whereas any validity-weighted or lexicographic integrator yields values well above 0.5; the metric measures a real behavioural phenomenon (magnitude sensitivity on count-tied trials) rather than model fit.

The design contains tally-TIE trials (each option wins exactly the same number of expert comparisons) that nevertheless carry a LARGE validity-weighted margin: base 7 / its mirror, where one option wins only on the .97 expert and the other only on the .53 expert. Tallying's softmax is exactly uniform whenever the two counts are equal, for ANY beta and epsilon, so the predicted proportion of choices for the option holding the high-validity cue is exactly 0.50 \u2014 a parameter-free prediction. AVAI acts on the continuous weighted difference (d \u2248 +0.66 with gamma=2), giving p \u2248 0.95\u20130.99 for that same option across its whole parameter range. I deliberately exclude the other tie structure (H1+L3 vs H2+L1, |d| \u2248 0.02) via the 0.30 threshold, because both theories predict chance there and it would only dilute the contrast. Each subject contributes 12 such trials, so per-subject binomial noise is small (var of the proportion \u2264 0.021 for Tallying, ~0.003 for AVAI), while the mean gap is ~0.47 \u2014 large mean separation with tight per-subject spread. The metric is well defined on a single subject's slice and on the pooled frame.
